Read History Go to My Account Log Out Interview NSIA has mobilised $1bn in third-party capital – Umar-Sadiq, MD/CEO … consolidates focus on catalysing investments and creating jobs The Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority (NSIA) has mobilised about $1 billion
Listen to this article Share … consolidates focus on catalysing investments and creating jobs The Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority (NSIA) has mobilised about $1 billion in third-party capital over the past decade, leveraging $400 million to $500 million in its own investments to attract funding for infrastructure and other critical sectors, its managing director and chief executive officer, Aminu Umar-Sadiq , has said. Speaking to Onyinye Nwachukwu , Abuja Bureau Chief at BusinessDay, on the sidelines of the 2026 IMF/World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, Umar-Sadiq said the Authority is shifting its focus from catalysing investment to creating jobs and delivering measurable economic impact. He outlined plans to scale a $300 million renewable energy fund, expand healthcare services, develop digital infrastructure and attract more private capital into large-scale projects. He also discussed efforts to finance Nigerian startups, reduce dependence on imports and position the country as a destination for global investment. EXCERPTS… First, could you walk us through NSIA’s participation at the 2026 IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings and share your key takeaways? Let me start by saying that NSIA has a long-standing and deep relationship with the World Bank Group. Over the past year, we have worked together on three key initiatives. The first is MedServe, our world-class oncology and diagnostics platform. We mobilised $24 million from the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the International Development Association (IDA), both part of the World Bank Group, in local-currency financing to support MedServe’s expansion. It is the first of its kind. The second is our distributed renewable energy platform in Nigeria, which we are developing alongside the International Solar Alliance, Africa50 and the World Bank. The World Bank has also contributed $20 million to the initiative. The third is INFRAGROW, our integrated, large-scale infrastructure financing platform, which we are co-developing with the World Bank, which is looking to contribute $500 million. These three engagements made it important for NSIA to participate in the Annual Meetings. One of our key priorities here has been to deepen our institutional relationship with the World Bank Group. We have held meetings with global directors of finance and infrastructure, as well as chief financial officers across MIGA, the World Bank and the IFC. The goal is to consolidate the work we are already doing together, strengthen those relationships and, importantly, lay the foundation for even greater collaboration going forward. The second is that NSIA is looking to ensure that we go beyond being catalytic to actually becoming a job creator for Nigeria. So, beyond conceptualising, developing and implementing pioneering propositions, and then mobilising capital towards those propositions, we want to now go a step further in ensuring that Nigerians actually feel the impact of activities that the Sovereign Wealth Fund is undertaking. And that job creation priority actually overlaps very strongly with one of the themes of this year’s Annual Meetings. The third area is AI, data and technology. You may be aware that earlier this year we launched Kasi Cloud, our hyperscale data centre. We also have an innovation prize and a venture capital platform seeded alongside JICA and BII to invest in Nigerian entrepreneurs developing innovative solutions, with equity as a preferred instrument. So, these three priorities — deepening our relationship with the World Bank Group, translating our catalytic investments into jobs, and expanding our investments in AI, data and technology — made our participation in these meetings particularly important. That said, there are several takeaways, but one key lesson is that we have a lot to learn from other developing economies. Many are grappling with the same challenges as Nigeria, from maximising the impact of scarce resources and deepening capital markets to mobilising private investment for infrastructure. It was valuable to hear how other countries are tackling these challenges and, more importantly, to consider how we can adapt those solutions to Nigeria’s realities. For me, that is one of the key outcomes of these meetings. The second was to evangelise on behalf of our country and show that Nigeria is open for business. We wanted to highlight the strong economic reforms this government has championed across foreign exchange, taxation, oil and gas, the capital market and currency convertibility, and encourage multilateral institutions and private sector businesses to see Nigeria as their gateway to the continent. I think that has been very important. Thirdly, it was about deepening our engagement with the World Bank ecosystem. Everyone is here — the DFIs, multilateral institutions, private sector players, foundations and philanthropic organisations. It’s almost a one-stop shop for networking and building relationships. For me, those were the three main outcomes. Nigeria has had a strong presence at these meetings, with top officials taking on prominent roles as panelists and session chairs. What does this say about Nigeria’s changing standing on the global stage? You feature prominently when you have something meaningful to say and successful case studies to share. I think Nigeria is enjoying that at the moment. We have successful investments and policy initiatives to show for it, and people now want to learn from our experience. Take, for instance, how NSIA has mobilised domestic capital for infrastructure through Medserve and InfraCredit, or built businesses from scratch, such as Medserve and RIPLE. There’s also Nigeria’s efforts to deepen its capital market and reforms around fuel subsidies and foreign exchange. People have studied these policies and want to understand what we’ve done. So, we’ve moved from being the ones learning from others to having experiences and successful initiatives that others want to learn from us. Job creation was a major theme at the meetings. You’ve also spoken about NSIA’s shift from catalysing investment to driving more direct job creation. What does this shift look like in practice, and how is it progressing? Job creation is fundamental to what we do, and we’re pursuing it through several initiatives. The first is that we are creating an institution called INFRAGROW, an integrated blended-finance platform designed to fund large-scale infrastructure projects through four ring-fenced facilities. The first is a project preparation facility to de-risk projects. The second is a viability gap facility to make critical infrastructure projects commercially viable. The third provides risk capital through equity investments to attract commercial banks and insurance companies. The fourth is a credit guarantee facility designed to bring in long-term, conservative capital once projects become operational. Together, these facilities will help us mobilise capital into INFRAGROW, and then be able to execute large-scale infrastructure projects despite financing constraints. In doing so, we expect to create significant jobs. We’re also looking at profitable, well-governed private-sector businesses that need capital to scale. By investing our own capital, we can attract additional funding to help these businesses grow into national champions. So, our focus is on using NSIA’s capital and convening power to mobilise more investment and get projects off the ground. NSIA is playing a key role in the energy sector, including the recently launched $300 million Nigeria Distributed Renewable Energy Fund with Africa50 and other partners. How much has been committed so far, when will investments begin to flow into projects, and how many Nigerians are expected to benefit? The fund is targeting $300 million at final close. We expect to reach $100 million very shortly, based on the commitments we have and advanced discussions with other partners, including NSIA, ISA, the World Bank and Africa50. With that initial $100 million, we intend to begin deploying capital immediately. We’re already engaging with pipeline projects to identify where the investments can go. Our goal is to build a successful portfolio that will help us attract more capital and reach the $300 million target. This fund is pioneering because we want to demonstrate that distributed renewable energy, particularly off-grid, point-of-use solutions, is an effective way to provide power in economies like ours. The impact goes beyond electricity access. These projects will create jobs during construction and implementation, while more affordable and reliable power will help businesses grow and create further employment. That’s why we’re excited about this fund. We want to start with $100 million and scale up to $300 million as we bring more partners on board. How will the fund work in practice, and how will projects be selected and financed? There are many power developers in Nigeria undertaking generation projects, particularly captive power projects that supply industrial and commercial customers. Many have secured some equity and debt financing but still lack the capital to complete their projects and begin construction. That’s where the fund comes in. By helping these projects get off the ground, we can create jobs during construction and operation. But the impact goes beyond the power plants themselves. And why this is important is that these businesses will be supplying electricity to industrial and commercial customers at lower costs than they currently pay, and once that happens, those customers can then improve their margins, expand operations and create more jobs. So, we’re looking at job creation from two angles: the power projects themselves and the businesses that benefit from more affordable electricity. Have you identified the projects? Oh, yes! We have a substantial pipeline of projects. Any investor looking to commit capital to a fund will want to see three things: a strong pipeline of projects, a capable management team and a sound governance structure. We’ve been able to attract leading partners because we have these elements in place. Our pipeline is bankable, and it needs to be several times the size of the fund to give us enough options as some projects may not make it through negotiations. Following the commissioning of Kasi Cloud’s data centre in Lekki, how much capacity is available to customers, what level of commercial activity has it attracted, and when do you expect the investment to start generating returns for NSIA? We’ve only just commissioned the data centre, and we’re focused on two things. First, we’re selling capacity to industrial clients, including telecoms companies and banks. Second, we’re preparing to expand. What we’ve commissioned is the first of three phases, so while we commercialise phase one, we’re also working towards phase two. For us, this is critical infrastructure for Nigeria. We shouldn’t have to export our data. We need data sovereignty, where data generated by Nigerians can be stored and processed here at home. This hyperscale data centre will help us build that capacity, ensuring that Nigeria has the digital infrastructure to support services such as AI and search, even if access to external systems is disrupted. Beyond being a business in its own right, it will also support the growth of Nigeria’s venture capital and telecoms industry. It’s an important enabler of the wider digital ecosystem, and we’re excited about what it can deliver. By the way, Kasi Cloud is a hyperscale data centre that processes digital requests. When you run a search, use a banking service or submit a prompt to an AI tool, the data centre can handle that processing here in Nigeria rather than sending it to facilities in places like Virginia or South Africa before the response comes back to you. That’s why this infrastructure is so important. Countries like the US and China are expanding their data centre capacity, and Nigeria needs to do the same to strengthen its data sovereignty and ensure more of the data generated here can be stored and processed locally. Does the project have a sovereign backing? Absolutely. As a sovereign wealth fund, our investments carry that sovereign backing. We manage funds for future generations of Nigerians, so that support is inherent in what we do. As a public-sector institution, we also have strong relationships with the ministries of finance, communications and power. That enables us to help navigate the permits and approvals required to deliver a complex project like this. NSIA is investing heavily in healthcare, particularly oncology and diagnostic centres across Nigeria. How many centres are currently operational, how much has been invested so far, and how is the programme reducing Nigerians’ need to seek cancer treatment abroad? We started by identifying gaps in the healthcare sector and developing solutions around three areas: oncology, diagnostics and medical manufacturing. We began with one oncology centre and two diagnostic centres as a proof of concept. This allowed us to test the entire model, from procurement and equipment costs to pricing, governance, patient experience, and recruiting and training clinical and non-clinical staff. We co-located the centres within teaching hospitals. Once we had refined the model, we moved to expansion in phases. The first phase involves 10 additional diagnostic centres, including two oncology centres, as well as three cardiac care centres or catheterisation laboratories. The total project size is over $200 million. Our priority now is to bring other development finance institutions into the funding structure so we can reduce the amount of our own capital tied up in the programme and eventually recycle it into other investments. We have 10 additional centres in the pipeline, which, together with the existing three, will bring the network to 13. We plan to operate these centres for another year or two, consolidate the model and then consider further expansion. Ultimately, our goal is to ensure that Nigerians have access to high-quality healthcare at affordable prices. We started with oncology, but over time, we also plan to expand into other areas, including nephrology and cardiology. The expansion programme is valued at $220 million and will be implemented in phases. We’ve invested about half of that so far. As we expand, we’ll deploy the remaining capital. The total programme is valued at about $220 million like I said. In terms of impact, the results have been significant. Nigerians can now access world-class equipment and specialists, including oncologists, therapists and medical physicists, at our centre at LUTH, at reasonable prices. What’s the status of the $50 million NSIA–JICA Impact Innovation Fund? Has a fund manager been appointed, and when do you expect the first investments to reach Nigerian startups? It’s important for us to find ways to support and fund Nigerian entrepreneurs, particularly young people, in local currency. NSIA already anchors several venture capital funds, including Ventures Platform, Ingressive Capital and LoftyInc, but we wanted to go a step further by creating our own fund. We’re particularly interested in sectors beyond fintech, such as healthtech, Insurtech and agritech, where innovative Nigerian startups also need capital. The idea is to bring together leading development finance institutions, including JICA and British International Investment (BII), to fund early-stage Nigerian businesses in local currency. The fund is valued at $50 million, with NSIA committing up to $20 million. We’ve secured $14 million from JICA and are working to conclude discussions with BII, as a co-investor. As you know, we have strong governance processes at NSIA and are running a transparent process to select a fund manager. We’re currently at the request-for-proposals stage, and the response from fund managers has been very encouraging. We hope to conclude the process next quarter and appoint a world-class manager to build the investment pipeline, deploy capital, support entrepreneurs in growing their businesses and raise additional funding to scale the fund. NSIA has positioned itself as a catalyst for private investment in infrastructure and other critical sectors. How much private capital did it mobilise in 2025, and what is its target for 2026? Over the past 10 years, we have deployed about $400 million to $500 million and mobilised approximately $1 billion in third-party capital. Our investments have also catalysed significant additional funding across initiatives we have established. For InfraCredit, for instance, our initial $25 million investment has helped attract about $400 million in tier-one and tier-two capital from institutions including AFC, InfraCo, KfW and, more recently, IFC. The same model applies to the Development Bank of Nigeria (DBN), the Nigeria Mortgage Refinance Company (NMRC), our infrastructure projects and the ammonia plants we are developing. MedServe is another example of how our initiatives can mobilise additional capital. Overall, our $400 million to $500 million in capital deployment has helped mobilise about $1 billion in third-party capital. That’s an important performance metric for us because it shows that we are stretching our capital further while delivering infrastructure projects. Take our distributed renewable energy platform, for example. NSIA is committing about $40 million. By the first close, we expect to mobilise an additional $60 million, bringing the total to $100 million. By the final close, we aim to raise that to $300 million, including $260 million in additional capital. It’s exciting because NSIA provides a fantastic vehicle for the government to mobilise private capital and channel it into infrastructure development. The ammonia plant project, involving Morocco’s OCP appears to have taken longer than expected. What is its current status, and when do you expect progress? The ammonia plant is an important project for us. We want to produce NPK fertiliser — nitrogen, phosphate and potash. Nigeria already produces urea, but we still import phosphate and potash. NSIA wants to change that by developing the capacity to produce phosphate locally. Our partnership with OCP Morocco is designed to establish an ammonia production facility and combine it with phosphoric acid to produce diammonium phosphate for Nigerian farmers. But a project of this scale involves several moving parts. You need gas, land, detailed feasibility studies, environmental and social impact assessments, about 20 permits, financing from both equity and debt investors, and offtake agreements. Bringing all these elements together takes time, particularly against the backdrop of COVID-19 and ongoing wars, which have made project development and financing more challenging. But we have kept at it. We have an excellent partner in Morocco’s OCP and a supportive regulatory environment. NNPC is also now involved, and we hope to reach the final stages of development soon. But projects of this scale take time, and this one is no exception. When do you expect the project to be completed? Hopefully, by this time next year, we should be reaching commercial close. That doesn’t mean construction will begin immediately. It’s a greenfield project, so we still need to reach financial close before construction can start, followed by operations. But I can assure you that, when completed, this will be a piece of infrastructure Nigeria can be proud of. NSIA has signed an agreement with Asset Green to explore a $496 million integrated dairy livestock and processing platform in Nigeria. What is the implementation timeline, how will the project reduce dairy imports, and when do you expect it to begin generating commercial returns? This is a very important project because Nigeria should not be importing finished milk. We should have an integrated dairy industry, from rearing and milking cows to processing and selling finished products. We have the land, the climate, the demand and the raw materials. What we need is the technical know-how, the right processing facilities and the structure to make a project of this scale viable. We are working with Asset Green and IFC to make this happen, and we’ve made significant progress on the development side. We are currently working on site and technology selection. Again, these development projects take time, but we continue to make good progress. With NSIA expanding its renewable energy portfolio and backing new power projects, what are the biggest obstacles to turning these investments into commercially viable businesses, particularly given Nigeria’s electricity market challenges? For NSIA, obstacles are disguised opportunities. Whenever you’re building something pioneering or transformative, challenges are inevitable. But we have the determination, ingenuity and capacity to find lasting solutions. These challenges may involve developing and selecting the right projects, currency convertibility, pricing, sponsors or project execution. We understand these risks and have the tools to manage them. Ultimately, delivering a successful portfolio with the capital raised at the first close has helped build investor confidence. When investors see that we can deliver results even under challenging conditions, they are confident to commit additional capital. That trust, backed by a proven track record, is what continues to attract further investment to us. We do know that NSIA’s portfolio spans infrastructure, healthcare, agriculture, energy and technology. Beyond growth in assets and financial returns, what indicators does the Authority use to measure the impact of its investments on jobs, household welfare and productivity, and what results can you point to so far? First of all, financial performance and returns on capital are critical. Second, we look at the infrastructure projects, platforms and funds we are developing with partners, and how many have reached financial close. Third is operational efficiency, meaning the kind of institution we are building, its capacity and its ability to execute. Fourth, there’s continental leadership. NSIA must continue to set the standard and serve as a beacon in Africa’s sovereign wealth fund landscape. Finally, NSIA operates within our public sector fabric. So, it’s important that beyond deploying capital and earning returns, that we are also supporting the government in advancing its own agenda. So, our ecosystem building, whether it’s in climate, whether it’s in healthcare, it’s about helping the government undertake complex consequential challenges. Finally, against the backdrop of global uncertainty over debt, interest rates, energy costs and emerging-market prospects, what specific investment opportunities did NSIA pursue during the Annual Meetings, and what new partnerships or capital commitments did you secure for Nigeria? Did you hold any concrete discussions with potential investors? Yes, we had many of those conversations around commitments. And there are many of those that we will be announcing in short order. I think for us, we have many innovative initiatives that are currently ongoing, for which we are in the process of mobilizing capital into. We are working on a storage initiative in order to make sure that our farmers post-harvest is able to store a lot of their staples. We want to proliferate storage, including silos, warehouses, bunkers, cold storage across the country so that farmers have storage capacity to reduce post-harvest losses. As you know, we are working on our VC platform, our DRE platform. We’re working on initiatives such as INFRAGROW, and forums like the Annual Meetings give us an opportunity to engage with development finance institutions, tell Nigeria’s investment story and mobilise capital. We’ve made tremendous progress on that front. It’s also an opportunity to learn from others and explore initiatives we can co-create to benefit Nigeria. The point on fiscal consolidation is very important, and it starts with discipline in how we borrow and spend. Any debt raised must go into productive investments that generate returns and expand the tax base, allowing the government to earn more revenue and service its debt. It’s important that as much as possible, debt should finance capital projects that drive GDP growth, generate returns, expand tax revenue and strengthen the government’s ability to repay. That discipline is critical. Debt itself is not necessarily a bad thing. What matters is whether the economy has the capacity to repay it and whether the funds are used for the purposes for which they were raised. Ideally, borrowing should be backed by a strong pipeline of projects that can deliver measurable economic returns. Debt should, as much as possible, finance capital projects that generate economic activity and revenue to support repayment. I believe the ministry of finance is very conscious of this and remains focused on it. NSIA is very active in this area. I think what gives us a special place in Nigeria’s financial architecture is the unique role we play in the country’s investment landscape.
